title: The history of bat sonar
tagline: From blinded bats in 1793 to a moth that jams their sonar: how people found out that bats see with sound.
intro: For 150 years, people knew that bats could fly in the dark and that their ears mattered, but nobody knew why. The answer needed a machine to detect sound we cannot hear. Once Harvard students had one, they found a whole sense, and later work found it in dolphins, birds, and a long arms race with moths. Some details, such as who first guessed what, are still argued over, and the sources say so where they differ.

eras.name: A sense nobody could name
eras.summary: Blinded bats still fly, deafened bats crash. For 150 years nobody can say how bats steer in the dark.

eras.name: Hearing the unheard
eras.summary: An ultrasound detector and a bat ear test at Harvard show that bats shout above our hearing and listen for the echoes.

eras.name: Dolphins, birds and hunting bats
eras.summary: Echolocation turns out to be a way of catching insects, and other animals use it too, from dolphins to cave birds.

eras.name: Brain maps and field studies
eras.summary: Researchers find how bats compensate for their own speed and how the cortex maps echo delay, and they record wild bats in the field.

eras.name: Moths, whispers and a fungus
eras.summary: Moths hear bats, tiger moths jam them, some bats whisper, and a new fungus begins to kill hibernating bats.

events.title: An Italian scientist blinds some bats and they still fly
events.text: Spallanzani caught wild bats, covered the eyes of some with an opaque coating and removed the eyes of one. They still flew without hitting obstacles and caught insects. He decided bats do not need sight to steer, but he could not say which sense they used. He published in 1794.
events.why: It showed that eyes are not what guides a bat in the dark.

events.title: A Swiss naturalist plugs bats' ears
events.text: Louis Jurine of Geneva heard about the experiments and tried plugging the ears of bats. They lost their way. Spallanzani repeated the test with better ear plugs and came to believe that hearing guided the flight. Jurine's results were published in 1798.
events.why: It pointed at the ear, but nobody knew what a bat could hear that we cannot.

events.title: Hahn repeats the old experiments
events.text: Hahn confirmed the findings of Spallanzani and Jurine. More than 30 years later Griffin repeated Hahn's obstacle tests and confirmed that bats with impaired hearing became disoriented.
events.why: It kept the puzzle alive: hearing mattered, yet bats seemed to fly in silence.

events.title: Maxim suggests bats steer by sound
events.text: Hiram Maxim proposed, independently, that bats avoid obstacles by sound. He guessed the pitch was below the range of human hearing. We now know it is above.
events.why: It was one of the first guesses that bats make a sound and listen for what comes back.

events.title: Hartridge guesses the sound is above our hearing
events.text: Hartridge proposed that bats use sounds pitched above the range of human hearing. His paper in the Journal of Physiology was titled "The avoidance of objects by bats in their flight". The idea could not be tested until a device to detect ultrasound existed.
events.why: He had the right answer about 18 years before anyone could check it.

events.title: A physics professor's ultrasound detector picks up bats
events.who: G. W. Pierce and Donald Griffin
events.text: George Washington Pierce, a physics professor, had built equipment to make and detect sounds above human hearing. Griffin, a student who banded bats, brought bats to his lab. The apparatus clicked and rattled whenever the bats were active. They reported the cries in the Journal of Mammalogy but were careful about saying what the cries were for.
events.why: It was the first proof that bats make sounds we cannot hear.

events.title: Galambos and Griffin show that bats steer by echoes
events.text: Galambos, a graduate student, recorded signals from bat ears and found their hearing reaches an octave or more above that of other animals. Together he and Griffin ran tests in which bats flew past obstacles. Every test pointed to the same answer: the bats shout, hear the echoes and steer by them. Their main paper came out in 1941.
events.why: It solved a puzzle that had stood for about 150 years.

events.title: Griffin gives the sense its name
events.text: Griffin's paper "Echolocation by blind men, bats and radar" appeared in the journal Science. It is the earliest use of the word "echolocation" in his bibliography. Many scientists of the day doubted that animals could do such a thing.
events.why: A name made it a field of study.

events.title: Bat calls turn out to be quick downward chirps
events.text: With a good condenser microphone and an oscilloscope, Griffin saw that bat cries were not noise bursts. They were chirps that swept down by about an octave in 1 or 2 milliseconds. Later work found that bats such as the little and big brown bat sweep from roughly 100 to 15 kilohertz.
events.why: The shape of the call, not just its pitch, carries the information.

events.title: A Marineland curator suspects dolphin sonar
events.text: McBride noticed that bottlenose dolphins could avoid nets and find gaps in them at night and in murky water. He suspected they had a sonar of their own. He wrote about it in 1956.
events.why: It opened the study of echolocation in the sea.

events.title: Echolocation by a cave-dwelling bird
events.where: Cave of the Guacharos, near Caripe, Venezuela
events.text: Griffin visited a cave where oilbirds nest in total darkness. Simple field tests showed they find their way with a crude form of echolocation. Their clicks are low enough for people to hear, at around 2 kilohertz.
events.why: It showed that echolocation is not only for bats.

events.title: Griffin hears the hunting buzz
events.text: Griffin made a crude ultrasound detector from a portable radio and listened to big brown bats over a pond. The put-put-put sped up as a bat closed in on a moth or beetle, to a buzz of up to 200 pulses a second. Until then, people thought echolocation was only a collision alarm.
events.why: It revealed that bats use echoes to catch small flying insects.

events.title: Echolocation differs from bat to bat
events.text: Griffin took his equipment to Panama and found that the orientation sounds of bats that eat insects, fruit, fish or blood differ a great deal. Fruit bats seemed to fly silently until better microphones showed they make faint sounds.
events.why: It showed that each kind of bat has its own style of echolocation.

events.title: Schevill and Lawrence study dolphin sound
events.where: Museum of Comparative Zoology, Harvard, USA
events.text: The husband-and-wife team of William Schevill and Barbara Lawrence made some of the first recordings of porpoise and whale sounds. They also carried out some of the early studies of dolphin sonar.
events.why: It laid groundwork for later proof of dolphin sonar.

events.title: Bats really do catch insects by echolocation
events.who: Donald Griffin, Frederic Webster and Charles Michael
events.text: Griffin's field recordings had left some critics unconvinced. A decade later, experiments with Frederic Webster settled it: some insect-eating bats use echolocation to catch small flying insects in the dark.
events.why: It moved the field from "can bats do it" to "what is it for".

events.title: Spallanzani's unpublished notes are published
events.text: Dijkgraaf, a Dutch comparative physiologist, published an account of Spallanzani's unpublished experiments on how bats sense objects in the journal Isis.
events.why: It filled in the story of the first experiments.

events.title: A blindfolded dolphin swims a maze
events.text: Norris and his team put rubber suction cups over the eyes of a bottlenose dolphin. It still swam through a maze of hanging pipes and avoided obstacles while making clicks. They guessed the clicks leave through the forehead, or melon.
events.why: It was the first conclusive demonstration of dolphin echolocation.

events.title: Moths with ears dodge bats
events.who: K. D. Roeder and A. E. Treat
events.text: Roeder and Treat showed that eared moths which dive or loop when they hear a bat are more likely to survive. Today we know moth ears evolved independently at least six times, and each one has only one to four sound-sensing cells.
events.why: It was the first look at the moth side of the arms race.

events.title: Horseshoe bats correct for their own speed
events.text: Schnitzler found that greater horseshoe bats lower the pitch of their call by about the amount that their own flight will raise the echo. That keeps the echo near the frequency they hear best, in a narrow band of the ear called the auditory fovea.
events.why: It showed how a bat can read speed from a sound.

events.title: Bat cortex has a map of distance
events.text: In the mustached bat, Suga and O'Neill found neurons in the auditory cortex that respond best when an echo arrives a particular time after the bat's own call. These cells are laid out in order of delay, so they form a map of target distance. A separate area has cells tuned to Doppler shift, which form a map of speed.
events.why: It showed how the brain turns echo delay into distance.

events.title: Call shape sorted by hunting style
events.text: Schnitzler and Kalko proposed four functional groups of insect-eating bats and showed that the shape of their calls matches the tasks each group does. Kalko's field work, with flash photography of bats in flight and ultrasound recorders, set the standard for studying wild bats.
events.why: It linked call design to where and how a bat hunts.

events.title: White-nose syndrome is found in New York
events.text: A photo from February 2006 shows hibernating bats with a white substance on their muzzles in a cave in east central New York. In March 2007, biologists saw unusual numbers of bats dying at five hibernation sites near Albany. The disease is caused by a fungus that infects bats while they hibernate.
events.why: It was the start of one of the worst wildlife diseases ever recorded.

events.title: Bats cry out loud
events.text: Surlykke and Kalko recorded 11 insect-eating bat species in Panama. Most calls were about 122 to 134 decibels at 10 centimetres from the mouth. Two water-trawling Noctilio bats were the loudest, at about 137 decibels on average.
events.why: It showed that bat calls are very loud, yet pitched above our hearing.

events.title: A tiger moth jams bat sonar
events.who: Aaron Corcoran, Jesse Barber and William Conner
events.text: The tiger moth Bertholdia trigona answers a bat's attack with bursts of clicks. A later study with big brown bats found that the bats often missed their prey by roughly 15 to 20 centimetres once they had met the clicking moth.
events.why: It is the only animal known to jam the sonar of its predator.

events.title: The white-nose fungus gets a name
events.text: The fungus found on the bats was formally named Geomyces destructans. It is now called Pseudogymnoascus destructans.
events.why: Naming the cause let researchers track and test it.

events.title: A bat that whispers to hunt moths
events.who: Holger Goerlitz, Hannah ter Hofstede and colleagues
events.text: The rare barbastelle bat echolocates up to 100 times more quietly than other bats. Moths can hear most bats from more than 30 metres away, but the barbastelle can get as close as 3.5 metres without being heard. Its calls reach less far, which is the price of the trick.
events.why: It showed that a bat can adapt its calls to moth hearing, at a cost in range.

events.title: Millions of bats lost
events.text: A review by a U.S. Geological Survey scientist estimated that white-nose syndrome had killed more than 5 million insect-eating bats. It had reached 19 U.S. states and four Canadian provinces, and the fungus was also found on hibernating bats in at least 12 European countries.
events.why: It showed how fast a disease of hibernating bats could spread.

events.title: A tribute to Elisabeth Kalko
events.text: A special journal issue marked the death of Kalko, who died on 26 September 2011 in Tanzania at age 49. Colleagues remembered her as a gifted naturalist whose work spanned echolocation, community ecology and bat-plant interactions. Griffin had called her the Jane Goodall of bats.
events.why: It honoured one of the great field biologists of echolocation.

facts: Bat calls recorded across species range from about 11 to 212 kilohertz, and measured loudness from about 60 to 140 decibels.
An echo delay of 1 millisecond means a target about 17 centimetres away.
Bottlenose dolphins can hear from about 100 hertz to 150 kilohertz, the widest range known for any mammal.
A moth's ear has only one to four sound-sensing cells, yet moths dive away from bats in time to survive.
The oilbird clicks at about 2 kilohertz, low enough for people to hear.
